annotations.text:
Five design languages for the control screen, not five coats of paint on the current one.

All six frames show the same moment so they can be compared honestly: connected, 78% battery, oven at 193.4 °C, target 193, Standard mode, 193° preset live. Real values, real range (180–225, marked past 215), real mode names.

What makes today's screen read as sci-fi is not the dial — it is four things at once: saturated orange on near-black, a glowing 26 pt arc, tracked-out caps (READY) and a neon green status dot. Each direction below drops all four and replaces them with a different idea of what an instrument looks like. Pick one and we take it the rest of the way — states, light and dark, charging, the Lock Screen card.

A · WERKSTATT — Braun functionalism

Warm grey chassis, matte plates, 4 pt corners everywhere, lowercase labels, one accent (vermilion) reserved for the one thing you set: the target. The dial becomes a printed linear scale — a solid bar for what the oven is, a vermilion index for what you asked for, a hatched band past 215 instead of a brown glow. Modes become a five-position switch.

Why: reads as a tool you'd buy, not an app you downloaded. Ages well.
Tradeoff: the big circular dial is gone, and with it drag-the-ring scrubbing — a linear scale needs a different gesture. Also a light-first design, so dark mode is real work rather than a token swap.

B · EDITORIAL — Swiss page, no chrome

No cards, no fills, no corners. Hairline rules and typography do all the work: the reading is set at 122 px in a display serif, and modes become a contents list. One ink-red accent, used four times on the whole screen.

Why: the most distinctive of the five, and the furthest from anything that looks like a gadget app. Very hard to make look cheap.
Tradeoff: the least conventional — tap targets are implied by rules rather than drawn, which asks more of the user. A serif in a hardware app is a taste call, so say early if it is not yours.

C · NATIVE — look like the phone, not like an app

Stock iOS: large title, inset grouped cards, a system slider for the target, a segmented control for presets, a checkmark list for modes. System colors, system type, system metrics. The accent only appears on controls.

Why: professional by disappearing. Fastest to build, free accessibility, Dynamic Type and light/dark, and it will still look right after the next iOS redesign.
Tradeoff: no character at all — nothing here says PAX, or says heat. And the temperature stops being the screen; it becomes a row in a card.

D · THERMAL — the oven as a column of heat

Stays dark, but warm graphite rather than black, and drops the ring entirely. The oven is a vertical vessel filled from cold (30 °C) to now, so a glance tells you how far through the warm-up you are — something the current arc cannot show, since it only starts at 180. Ember gradient in the column, nowhere else. Flat keys, 3 pt corners, the live mode lit along one edge.

Why: the only direction where the main graphic carries information the number doesn't. Keeps the dark screen you already have.
Tradeoff: closest to today, so it is the smallest change of the five — if the goal is "not that", this may not go far enough. Condensed type needs care at small sizes.

E · INSTRUMENT — a printed gauge, not a glowing one

Keeps the circle, throws away the neon: an ivory face with every degree printed, a brushed steel bezel, a slender red needle for the oven and a red bezel index for your target — exactly how a real gauge separates "is" from "set". The digital reading sits in a window below the hub. Presets are printed chips; modes are a selector with the live position raised.

Why: keeps the dial you clearly like as the identity of the app, while looking machined rather than animated. Charging and battery have obvious homes as sub-dials.
Tradeoff: the most decorative of the five, and skeuomorphic — done badly this goes kitsch fast. Also the most work to build and animate well.
